column1: # What a log line means, in words.
# One literal string per row, and what it means when it turns up. Read by
# `bin/aurade-explain`, which is what turns four hundred lines of kernel
# messages into two sentences somebody can act on.
#   key       the literal that appears in the log, byte for byte. A literal and
#             never a pattern: a thousand of them match in one pass, anybody
#             can search for one and find the driver that prints it, and it
#   source    kernel, pacman, systemd, efi, luks, installer. `--source` narrows
#             a scan to one of these.
#             fault  something is broken and the reader has to do something
#             warn   something is degraded and will probably still work
#             note   this looks alarming and is normal. Hidden unless --all.
#   what      what happened. One or two sentences. For a note, lead with the
#             reassurance, the same way a failure screen leads with the disk.
#   do        what to do, in one sentence, or `-` when the honest answer is
#   evidence  where the string is emitted, so an entry can be checked rather
#             than believed. For kernel rows this is `path:line` in the kernel
#             source, and `tools/verify-hardware-notes.sh` checks every one of
#             them against a real tree. A row that nothing emits is worse than
#             no row at all, because it never fires and so is never noticed.
# The voice is the one in UI_CONTRACT.md, and it applies here harder than
# anywhere else: this file is read by somebody who is already worried. No
# jargon they have not already got, no hexadecimal, and never an account of
# how the computer knows. Say what happened, then say what to do.
# The `note` rows are not filler. Most of what looks frightening in a kernel
# log is normal, and somebody who cannot tell which is which pastes all four
# hundred lines somewhere and waits. Saying "nothing is wrong" about the right
# lines is the half of this file that saves a person an evening.

column4: The drive stopped answering, so Linux reset it and carried on.
column5: Copy anything you care about off this drive before you install. A drive that does this is often on its way out.

column4: The drive stopped responding altogether and Linux is restarting it.
column5: Copy anything you care about off this drive before you install.

column4: The drive did not come back after a reset.
column5: Shut the computer down fully, wait ten seconds, then start it again. A restart alone does not always power the drive down.

column4: The drive refused a power saving setting Linux asked for.
column5: On some laptops the drive then stops answering later in the install. Add nvme_core.default_ps_max_latency_us=0 to the boot options and try again.

column4: Nothing is wrong. The drive did not report its own health figures.
The drive reported an error and the command had to be retried.
column5: Check the SATA cable at both ends first. A loose or worn cable causes this far more often than a failing drive does.

column4: Linux reset the connection to the drive to get it answering again.
column5: Check the SATA cable at both ends. One of these on its own is normal, and a run of them is not.

column4: Nothing is wrong. There is no drive attached to that port.
Nothing is wrong. The drive is taking its time to wake up and Linux is waiting for it.
Linux slowed the connection to the drive down to keep it stable.
column5: The drive will work and it will be slower. A different cable usually fixes it.

column1: NCQ disabled due to excessive errors
column4: Linux turned off a speed feature because the drive kept getting it wrong.
column5: The drive will work and it will be slower. Check the cable, then check the drive for faults.

column4: The drive stopped identifying itself the way it did a moment ago.
column5: Copy anything you care about off this drive. Do not install onto it until you have checked it for faults.

column4: The connection to the drive did not come back after the computer woke up.
column5: Restart the computer rather than waking it. This is a firmware problem and a full restart clears it.

column4: Nothing is wrong. The drive answered an old question in an old way.
A USB device did not answer when Linux asked what it was.
column5: Move it to a different USB socket, and use one on the computer itself rather than a hub.

column4: A USB device is plugged in and Linux cannot talk to it.
column5: Move it to a different USB socket. If it is the drive you started the installer from, write the image again onto a different USB stick.

column1: Cannot enable. Maybe the USB cable is bad
column4: A USB device kept failing to start.
column5: Try a different cable and a different socket. On a USB drive this is usually the cable.

column1: Card is consuming too much power
column4: The card reader cut power to the card to protect the computer.
column5: Take the card out and put it back in. If it happens again the card is faulty.

column4: The card reader stopped answering while it was being used.
column5: Take the card out and put it back in. Do not install onto a card that does this.

column4: Part of the disk could not be read or written.
column5: Copy anything you care about off this disk now. Do not install onto it.

column4: An existing Linux filesystem on one of these disks is damaged.
column5: This does not stop the install. Check that filesystem with fsck before you trust anything on it.

column4: A Btrfs filesystem reported an error.
column5: Save a report. If this is the disk being installed to, start the install again from the beginning.

column4: A Btrfs filesystem is inconsistent with itself.
column5: This usually follows a power cut or a failing disk. Check the disk for faults before installing onto it.

column4: Btrfs read data back and it was not what was written.
column5: The disk is corrupting data. Do not install onto it.

column4: A Btrfs filesystem could not be opened at all.
column5: Save a report before doing anything else. Mounting it again will not help.

column1: failed to read the system array
column4: The part of the Btrfs filesystem that says where everything is could not be read.
column5: Save a report. Do not write anything else to this disk.

column4: Nothing is wrong. The drive did not say whether it caches writes, so Linux assumed the safe answer.
Nothing is wrong. Linux picked the safe assumption about how the drive caches writes.
Nothing is wrong. The processor reported an interrupt problem and carried on.

column1: Uhhuh. NMI received for unknown reason
column4: Nothing is wrong. The computer's firmware sent Linux a signal it does not recognise.

column1: Dazed and confused, but trying to continue
column4: Nothing is wrong. That is the kernel's own wording for a signal it does not recognise, and it carried on.
Nothing is wrong. Linux turned off a timer feature this processor gets wrong.
Nothing is wrong. Linux switched to a different clock because the processor's own one drifted.
Nothing is wrong. Linux slowed its own measuring down to stay out of the way.
The processor or the memory reported a real hardware fault.
column5: Run a memory test before installing. This is one of the few messages here that is never noise.

column4: The processor recorded a hardware fault and kept going.
column5: Run a memory test before installing.

column4: Nothing is wrong with your computer. Its firmware has a bug in it and Linux worked around it.
Nothing is wrong with your computer. Its firmware did something out of spec and Linux carried on.
Nothing is wrong. The firmware referred to something that is not there and Linux skipped it.
Nothing is wrong. A firmware routine failed and Linux stopped running it.
The computer ran out of memory and Linux stopped a program to get some back.
column5: Close everything else and start the install again. If it happens again, this computer does not have enough memory for it.

column4: Something ran out of the memory it was allowed to use.
column5: Close everything else and start the install again.

column4: The graphics card reported a fault and Linux recovered from it.
column5: The screen may have flickered. If it keeps happening, start the installer in safe graphics mode.

column4: Nothing is wrong. The graphics card stopped for a moment and picked itself back up.
The graphics card locked up and Linux restarted it.
column5: The screen may have gone black for a second. If it keeps happening, start the installer in safe graphics mode.

column4: The graphics card locked up and Linux restarted it.
column5: If it keeps happening, start the installer in safe graphics mode.

column4: A piece of hardware asked for firmware that is not on this system.
column5: Wireless and graphics are the usual ones. Everything else will install, and that device will not work until its firmware is installed.

column4: Linux could not reach the firmware settings store.
column5: The install will finish, and this computer may not offer AuraDE in its boot menu afterwards.
